activities.anchor: eating other organisms from the inside of a gut
activities.caption: each clause does work — match it to its exclusion
activities.name: zooClauseMatch

config.prompt: The four-clause definition — match each clause to the look-alike it excludes:

pairs.right: single-celled protists — an amoeba engulfs food just as a white blood cell does
plants (photosynthesis) and fungi (which digest outside their bodies and absorb)
most plants and fungi, which cannot commute to their food
every other kingdom — a hollow ball of cells is the developmental signature nothing else shares

config.why: Animals are monophyletic — all descendants of one multicellular ancestor that lived roughly 600–700 million years ago — and the definition is that ancestor's inheritance list.

activities.anchor: the reef is an animal city
activities.caption: animal or not? file the look-alikes
activities.name: zooWhoSort

config.prompt: The definition is developmental and nutritional, not intuitive — file each case:

items.label: sponges — no nerves, no gut, no symmetry

config.why: Roughly three-quarters of described animal species are arthropods; and not everything that moves and eats is an animal — Euglena is a protist.

config.prompt: The current reconstruction of the animal origin, in order:
items: Division of labour — some cells specialise in reproduction, others in feeding or structure
A colony becomes an individual — and a body can grow large, live longer than its cells, and let some cells die to protect the rest
config.why: The transition happened at least half a dozen times independently — in animals, plants, fungi, and several algal and slime-mould lineages — so the first step is not astronomically hard; the parts list existed before the building.

activities.anchor: as far down its own road as we are down ours
activities.caption: one line of this museum placard is wrong
activities.name: zooPlacardSpot

config.prompt: One line of this museum placard is wrong — click it:
lines: Choanoflagellates are single-celled protists — the closest living relatives of animals.
Their colonies show multicellularity can evolve from single cells.
Their genomes contain many of the signalling and adhesion genes animals later used to build bodies.
They are the actual ancestors of animals — a living snapshot of our lineage.
Modern choanoflagellate cells even resemble sponge collar cells.
config.correction: They are our closest living relatives — a different claim: both lineages have been evolving separately since their common ancestor some 600–700 million years ago; their value is as evidence about the ancestor's toolkit, not as the ancestor itself.
config.why: The modern choanoflagellate has its own 600-million-year history of change — evidence about the kit, not a snapshot of the road.

activities.anchor: water flows through them in any direction
activities.caption: radial vs bilateral — the first fork
activities.name: zooSymCompare

config.prompt: Symmetry is the first fork — drag the divider:

before.label: radial symmetry
before.text: every vertical plane is a mirror plane — ideal for meeting the world from all sides equally: drifting, sessile, or drifting-while-armed like the tentacled medusa

after.label: bilateral symmetry
after.text: one mirror plane only, splitting left from right — the symmetry of directed movement, where sensors and processors cluster at the end that meets the world first (cephalisation tracks bilaterality across the tree)

config.why: Sponges sit before the fork — asymmetrical, with no direction special — and the tissue-layer fork follows: diploblasts live with two layers, triploblasts add mesoderm, the invention of powerful movement.

activities.caption: name the three cavity plans
activities.name: zooCavCloze

config.text: Triploblasts divide by what lies between gut and body wall: %%0%% (flatworms — no cavity, so diffusion must reach every cell); %%1%% (roundworms — a cavity partly lined with mesoderm); %%2%% (annelids, molluscs, arthropods, chordates — a cavity fully lined with mesoderm).
config.hint: No cavity, partly lined, fully lined.

activities.anchor: the master regulators that tell each segment
activities.caption: true or false — the ancient patterning grammar
activities.name: zooHoxJudge

statements.s: Hox genes are arranged on the chromosome in the order they are expressed along the body.
statements.why: The chromosome order matches the anterior–posterior order — one of biology's great discoveries.

statements.s: Swap a fly Hox gene for its mouse counterpart and the mouse builds a fly.
statements.why: The reverse: put the mouse gene in the fly and the fly largely builds a fly — the grammar is conserved, the reading is local.

statements.s: A vertebrate's back develops where an insect's belly would.
statements.why: The dorsal–ventral machinery is so deeply conserved that the insects simply evolved upside down relative to us.

statements.s: 'Body plan' is a metaphor rather than a scientific concept.
statements.why: Beneath wildly different bodies runs one ancient patterning grammar — which is exactly why it is a concept and not a metaphor.

activities.anchor: the Burgess Shale's exquisitely preserved oddballs
activities.caption: bet the phylum count
activities.name: zooPhylaEst

config.prompt: Nearly all animal phyla appeared by the Cambrian, over 500 million years ago. Roughly how many phyla exist today?
config.why: Roughly thirty — and no new phylum-level body plan has clearly succeeded since the Palaeozoic: sponges kept filter-feeding, arthropods ran segmentation into an exoskeleton empire, and our chordate lineage bet on a stiff internal rod that became the backbone.
config.context: about thirty — the animal kingdom's diversity is mostly remixing of early engineering decisions
